title: How to Write Verifiable Requirements
excerpt: Most "unverifiable" requirements share the same three root causes. Here's how to catch them before review.
body:
A requirement is verifiable when there's an unambiguous, practical way to confirm — through inspection, test, analysis, or demonstration — that it's been met. Most requirements that fail this test fall into one of three patterns.

The first is subjective language: words like "user-friendly," "fast," or "robust" that mean something different to every reader. "The system shall respond quickly" isn't verifiable; "The system shall return search results within 2 seconds for 95% of queries under normal load" is.

The second is compound requirements — two or more distinct needs bundled into one statement, joined by "and" or "or." If a reviewer can't point to a single pass/fail outcome, split it into separate requirements.

The third, and the one that survives review most often, is missing the condition under which the requirement applies. "The system shall log all failed login attempts" sounds fine until someone asks: logged where, retained for how long, visible to whom? A verifiable requirement states its own boundary conditions rather than leaving them implicit.

Catching these three patterns during self-review, before a requirement ever reaches a formal walkthrough, is one of the fastest ways to cut review cycles — and it's exactly what the IREB CPRE quality criteria are built to test.

title: Requirements Review Checklist
excerpt: A practical, print-ready checklist covering the six IREB CPRE quality criteria.
body:
Before a requirement goes into a formal review, run it through these six checks — drawn directly from the IREB CPRE quality criteria for individual requirements.

1. Unambiguous — Could two competent readers interpret this differently? If there's any doubt, it fails this check regardless of how confident the author is.

2. Verifiable — Is there a concrete, practical way to confirm this has been met? If verifying it would require a subjective judgment call, rewrite it with a measurable condition.

3. Complete — Does the requirement stand on its own, or does it silently depend on information that lives somewhere else? A requirement that only makes sense next to a diagram nobody's attached yet isn't complete.

4. Consistent — Does it contradict another requirement elsewhere in the same document, even partially? This is the check most often skipped under time pressure, and the one that causes the most rework later.

5. Feasible — Can this actually be built within the known constraints (budget, technology, timeline)? A requirement can be perfectly well-written and still be infeasible.

6. Necessary — Does this trace back to an actual stakeholder need, or did it get added because it seemed reasonable at the time? Requirements without a traceable source are the first candidates for scope creep.

A requirement that passes all six isn't guaranteed to be right — but one that fails any of them is guaranteed to cause a problem later, just later enough that it's more expensive to fix.

title: ASPICE Traceability Essentials
excerpt: What SWE.1 traceability evidence actually needs to show — and the gaps assessors flag most often.
body:
SWE.1 (Software Requirements Analysis) asks for bidirectional traceability between customer requirements and software requirements — and between software requirements and later work products (architecture, test cases). The intent isn't paperwork for its own sake; it's the ability to answer two questions quickly: if a customer requirement changes, what software requirements are affected? And if a software requirement exists, which customer need justifies it?

The gap assessors flag most often isn't missing links — teams usually have a traceability matrix. It's stale links: a requirement gets revised during development, but the trace to its test case or parent requirement never gets updated, so the matrix technically exists but no longer reflects reality. A traceability matrix that hasn't been touched since the requirements freeze is a bigger red flag than a smaller matrix that's visibly current.

The second most common gap is traceability that only runs one direction. Being able to go from customer requirement down to software requirement is necessary but not sufficient — assessors will specifically ask you to go the other way, from a software requirement or a test case back up to the customer need it satisfies. If that direction requires manual searching rather than a maintained link, it's a finding waiting to happen.

The third is orphaned software requirements — ones with no upward trace at all. These usually enter the system informally (a developer's own assumption, a verbal request that never got documented as a customer requirement) and are exactly the ones assessors ask about first, because they're the easiest to spot and the hardest to justify on the spot.

title: MBSE Starter Guide
excerpt: Moving from document-based to model-based systems engineering, one diagram at a time.
body:
The hardest part of adopting MBSE isn't learning SysML notation — it's the shift in what counts as the authoritative source of truth. In a document-based approach, the Word document or spreadsheet is the real artifact, and any diagram is just an illustration of it. In MBSE, the model is the real artifact, and documents (if they exist at all) are generated views of it.

Teams that struggle with the transition usually try to adopt the whole method at once — full SysML, every diagram type, a complete model from day one. A more workable starting point is picking one recurring pain point and modeling just that. If requirements traceability is the actual problem, start with a requirements diagram linking to a small set of use cases, and prove that the model stays more current than the spreadsheet it replaces before expanding further.

The second practical starting point is the block definition diagram (BDD) for system decomposition — it maps closely to how most engineers already think about a system's structure, making it a natural first diagram type rather than the more abstraction-heavy behavioral diagrams (sequence, state machine).

Whichever diagram you start with, the test of whether MBSE is actually working isn't whether the diagrams look right — it's whether someone can answer a real engineering question faster from the model than they could have from the old documents. If that's not yet true for your first modeled subsystem, that's a sign to adjust scope before expanding it.

title: AI Prompt Templates for Requirements Engineers
excerpt: Five prompt patterns that hold up to IREB CPRE quality criteria, not just "sound good."
body:
A generic "improve this requirement" prompt tends to produce text that reads better without actually becoming more verifiable — the underlying ambiguity is often just rephrased more smoothly. The patterns below ask for something more specific than "improve it," which is what makes the output usable in a real review rather than something that needs re-checking anyway.

1. Ambiguity scan: "List every word or phrase in this requirement that could reasonably be interpreted two different ways, and suggest a specific replacement for each." This produces a checklist you can act on line by line, rather than a single rewritten paragraph you have to trust wholesale.

2. Verifiability test: "Describe exactly how someone would confirm this requirement has been met — what they would inspect, measure, or test. If you can't describe a concrete method, say so explicitly." Asking the model to admit when it can't verify something is what prevents it from confidently inventing a plausible-sounding but hollow verification method.

3. Compound-requirement split: "Does this requirement contain more than one independently testable condition? If so, split it into separate numbered requirements." Useful for catching "and"-joined requirements that read as one idea but need two pass/fail outcomes.

4. Missing-condition check: "What boundary conditions, exceptions, or contexts does this requirement leave unstated that a reviewer would need to ask about?" This surfaces the implicit assumptions that usually only come up during a live walkthrough.

5. Consistency check against a second requirement: "Do these two requirements conflict, even partially, under any interpretation?" Pasting requirement pairs rather than a whole document keeps the model's attention narrow enough to actually catch contradictions instead of skimming past them.

None of these replace a human reviewer — but each produces something specific enough to check against the IREB CPRE quality criteria, rather than a rewrite you have to take on faith.

title: CPRE vs Systems Engineering: What Should You Learn First?
excerpt: They're complementary, not competing — but the order you learn them in matters.
body:
Requirements engineering (IREB CPRE) and systems engineering (INCOSE-aligned) overlap enough that people often ask which one to learn first, as if picking one makes the other redundant. They don't compete — CPRE goes deep on eliciting, specifying, and validating requirements themselves; systems engineering takes those requirements as an input and covers how they flow into architecture, verification, and the full system lifecycle. Neither is a subset of the other.

The order that tends to work better in practice: start with CPRE if your day-to-day work is closer to gathering and specifying what a system should do — business analysts, product owners, and requirements engineers on a single-discipline team usually get value faster from CPRE Foundation, since it directly improves the artifacts they're already producing every week.

Start with systems engineering fundamentals first if you're already working across multiple disciplines (hardware, software, mechanical) on a complex system, where the requirements themselves are less often the bottleneck than getting them to flow correctly into architecture and verification across teams. In that context, systems engineering gives you the framework CPRE's requirements slot into.

If you're genuinely unsure which describes your situation, CPRE Foundation is the lower-commitment starting point (shorter, narrower scope) and its content directly strengthens systems engineering work later — the reverse isn't as true, since systems engineering fundamentals assumes you already have reasonably solid requirements to work with.
